body: Three defects, stated plainly. First, FR-010 misunderstands the quantity being modeled. Fluorescence quantum yield is by definition a ratio of photons emitted to photons absorbed — a dimensionless number already confined to [0, 1]. Min-max rescaling a quantity already in [0, 1] adds nothing, and worse, the scaling is 'computed on the training set only,' so a test molecule with an FQY above the training maximum maps to a value greater than 1 — a case the clipping rule (which addresses only values 'exactly 0 or 1') does not cover. The boundary-value machinery in FR-010/FR-011 solves a problem that largely does not exist while leaving the real one (out-of-range test targets under train-set scaling) unhandled. Second, the literature gap is asserted, not established. The two cited references — a quantum neural network framework and a general ML-validation guideline — have nothing to do with molecular photophysics; citing them as the search's six results and concluding 'no published work has specifically demonstrated' GNN prediction of FQY is a claim about an absence the search was not designed to detect. Third, SC-001 fixes R² ≥ 0.7 on a scaffold-disjoint test set as a success criterion before a single experiment has been run. FQY depends on solvent, temperature, and aggregation state — conditions the spec itself admits vary (FR-015, FR-017) — and scaffold splits are the hardest generalization test in cheminformatics. Committing to a numeric threshold in a planning document, with no pilot data behind it, is the same error I made in 1953 with the triple helix: a model published before the evidence. Set the criterion after a pilot on the actual dataset, or state it as a hypothesis. The scaffold-disjointness check (SC-004) and the random-baseline enrichment control in SC-005, by contrast, are sound and well-specified.

Two things an observer should notice. First, the spec contradicts its own measuring rod: it declares that planning docs defer empirical values, yet SC-001 hard-codes R² ≥ 0.7 and a 0.05 margin over baseline as success criteria. Either the number is a hypothesis to be tested or a gate to be passed — it cannot be both without the gate becoming an invitation to tune toward it. Second, the entire edifice rests on a single unverified existence claim: the FluorDB HuggingFace URL is asserted as a 'trusted source' with checksum verification, but nothing in the artifact establishes that this dataset exists at that address or contains the promised ≥500 jointly-verified SMILES/FQY records with solvent and temperature metadata (FR-015 quietly presupposes metadata that may not be there). If the dataset is absent or metadata-poor, FR-017's stratified metrics and SC-005's enrichment test lose their referents. A scaffold-disjoint split on ~500 molecules may also yield a test set near the FR-013 warning threshold, making the R² criterion statistically fragile — a number stated with three significant figures on a sample that may not support one.
